questions.q: Why does the team create a new, scoped GPO instead of editing the Default Domain Policy directly to apply the Windows hardening baseline?
options: Group Policy only applies to servers, never to workstations

A new GPO scoped through security filtering and OU targeting can be rolled out and rolled back in a controlled way, while editing the Default Domain Policy applies everywhere at once with no clean way back
Editing the Default Domain Policy is required by the CIS Benchmark
The Default Domain Policy cannot contain any security settings
questions.explain: A dedicated, scoped GPO gives controlled rollout and rollback; the Default Domain Policy applies org-wide immediately with no equivalent safety margin.

questions.q: What does enabling Credential Guard accomplish as part of the Windows baseline?
options: It disables all local administrator accounts on every endpoint
It replaces the need for any Conditional Access policy
It isolates LSA secrets in a protected memory space so malware that gains local admin still can't read cached credentials
It only works on Linux servers, not Windows
questions.explain: Credential Guard protects LSA secrets even from a process with local admin rights, which is exactly the privilege level most credential-theft attacks rely on.

questions.q: Why is the Linux remediation written as an Ansible playbook instead of applied by hand on each of the forty servers?
options: Manual changes are always faster and safer than automation
Ansible is the only tool capable of changing a sysctl parameter
CIS Benchmarks cannot be applied to Linux systems at all
A playbook makes the baseline repeatable, version-controlled, and reusable the next time a Linux server is provisioned, instead of a one-off manual pass
questions.explain: Writing the remediation as code gives the same controls-as-code benefits Chapter 7 covers: repeatability, version history, and reuse.

questions.q: What is the purpose of running the ASR rules in audit mode and the Ansible changes in a --check dry run against a 150-machine pilot group first?
options: To permanently disable the hardening baseline for that pilot group
Audit mode has no practical effect on testing accuracy
To skip the need for any exception process later
To surface real false positives, like a broken actuarial cron job and a blocked legacy spreadsheet, before enforcement affects anyone's actual work
questions.explain: Audit/dry-run testing on a pilot group catches real problems in logs before they become outages for the whole fleet.

questions.q: How does the team handle the actuarial cron job and the finance team's macro-enabled spreadsheet once the pilot audit surfaces them?
options: By abandoning the hardening rollout entirely
As documented, owned, time-limited exceptions — one rewritten within a week, the other logged with an owner and an expiration tied to a replacement project, reviewed quarterly
By silently excluding those two systems from the baseline forever with no tracking
By enforcing the baseline anyway and accepting the breakage
questions.explain: A real exception process names an owner and an expiration instead of leaving an open-ended, untracked carve-out in the baseline.
